job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Adam Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at 6:40 and take the bus along Northgate Road to a small haulage firm, where I'm the junior bookkeeper. I started in August, after my accounting degree. I match delivery invoices to purchase orders in a big spreadsheet and chase drivers for missing signatures. I share a flat with two guys I found online, and after work I mostly cook pasta and open my loan letters, which I then close again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave things alone. Our firm still wants paper delivery notes and a human to check them. At the pub I'd say software has been promising to replace accountants since before I was born, and we're still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in the short run. My boss, Mr Petrov, doesn't trust anything he can't print. But I worry about money more than AI. My loan repayments take a third of my pay and I have maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do. I'd stay at the haulage firm, finish the bookkeeping certificate Mr Petrov agreed to part-fund, and not touch any AI tool. I'd try to save 60 a month, which is silly, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's a steady, boring feeling, like walking uphill with a bag of bricks. AI isn't the brick. The student loan is, and nobody in government seems bothered about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI isn't the brick. What would ease the debt, if anything could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower interest rate, honestly, and proper pay. We're on the minimum entry rate and the firm made a profit this year. I think workers should be able to bargain for more, and the government should cap what loan companies charge us. I can't fix it on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you want to try any AI tools, even in a world where it's all hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen colleagues paste client details into those chatbots, and nobody knows where it goes. I'd rather do things slowly and correctly. Plus every free tool turns into a paid one, and I can't afford another subscription.

say: Software has promised to replace accountants for decades, and **we're still here**.
Our firm still wants paper delivery notes and a **human** checking each one.
think: My real worry is the **loan repayments**, which take a third of my pay.
I have about **three weeks** of savings, so one bad month would hurt.
do: Stay at the **haulage firm** and finish the part-funded bookkeeping certificate.
Try to save **60 a month**, even if it feels tiny.
feel: Tired and weighed down, but the **debt** is the weight, not AI.
S0.quote: AI isn't the brick. The student loan is, and nobody in government seems bothered about that.
fieldNote: **Blames** lenders and low pay far more than technology, which fits his left-leaning view.
Says he's fine on AI but admits he has under a month of savings.
Refuses AI tools on **privacy** and cost grounds, not fear.

steps.text: Stay at the haulage firm and keep matching invoices
Put 60 a month into a separate savings account
Back the student loan interest cap in the next election

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another excuse for firms to cut people and call it progress. Invoice matching, payment checking and data entry are the first things software takes. That's my whole job right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared that the haulage firm never replaces whoever leaves. Mr Petrov has talked about 'trying a package' for reconciling accounts. If he buys it, there's me, and there's Dilek in payroll, and one of us goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Petrov to put in writing that any new software won't cost jobs. I'd join the general union, because on my own I'm nothing. I'd keep applying quietly to council and hospital finance jobs. The public sector is slower but stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold in the stomach. I've just got my first real job after three years of living on lentils, and now the ground feels like it's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the software yourself, so you'd be the one who knows it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what everyone says, learn it. But I'm slow with new systems and I'd rather be thorough than fast. If I'm honest I'd do the opposite: stay out of it and hope someone senior sees that rushing creates errors. I know that's risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the union route doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I take whatever pays, even warehouse work at night. I'd rather lose a bit of pride than miss rent. My two flatmates would be out in two months if I couldn't pay, and that's on my conscience as well.

say: This is **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress.
Invoice matching and data entry go first, and that's **my whole job**.
think: If Mr Petrov (my boss) buys reconciliation software, **one of two** clerks goes.
I'd rather stay **thorough** than fast, though I know that's risky.
do: Join the **general union** and ask for no-job-loss terms in writing.
Quietly apply to **council and hospital** finance jobs.
feel: A **cold feeling** in my stomach, just after finally landing a real job.
S1.quote: I've just got my first real job after three years of living on lentils, and now the ground feels like it's moving.
fieldNote: Strong **union** instinct: his first move is collective, not personal upskilling.
**Resistance** to new tools is a stated choice, though he knows the risk.
Feels **responsible** for flatmates if his pay stopped.

steps.text: Join the general union and attend the next branch meeting
Apply for three council and hospital finance posts a month
Ask Mr Petrov for written terms before any new software arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it happens by 2028 I'd say we're not ready and nobody asked us. Public pressure should force governments to act, not a handful of tech bosses. I'd be loud about regulation, because there won't be time to be polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm done. I'd have paid maybe a fifth of my loan, and the firm would have no reason to keep a junior bookkeeper when software does it for free. Two years is nothing. And a degree with a pass and no internship isn't going to save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no phone upgrade, no train home at Christmas, and I'd sell my laptop's spare parts if I had any. I'd go to every union and community meeting about guaranteed income. I'd also ask my mum if I could move back, although she's in a one-bedroom flat and I really don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like standing on a platform watching a train arrive and having no ticket. I'd probably be sleeping badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay the minimum and stop trying to get ahead. If everyone's job goes, they can't chase millions of people for repayment, but I'd never count on that. It's a hope, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your flatmates or colleagues would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dilek in payroll. She's 51 and has two kids, and she's had this job for 20 years. She doesn't even use email properly. I'd feel guilty that I'm young and she's the one who'd really be flattened.

say: Nobody asked us, so **public pressure** must force governments to act.
I'd be loud about **regulation**, because there's no time to be polite.
think: Two years is **nothing**, and the firm has no reason to keep a junior clerk.
My plain pass degree and **no internship** won't protect me.
do: Cut every extra, including the Christmas **train home** and any phone upgrade.
Go to union meetings about **guaranteed income**, and ask my mum about moving back.
feel: Like standing on a platform with **no ticket**, sleeping badly.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. And a degree with a pass and no internship isn't going to save me.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** within two years and has no cushion, so alarmed fits.
Moves from **personal fear** to concern for Dilek, an older colleague.
Looks to **government** and unions, with little faith in firms.

steps.text: Pay only the minimum on the student loan and stop extra payments
Attend every union meeting about guaranteed income
Ask my mum whether I can move into her flat
Lobby my local representative for a regulation bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say there's time to organise. Unions should be pushing for shorter weeks and retraining paid by employers. I'd say it loudly online, but I'm no influencer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years feels like enough to be hurt slowly rather than all at once. I'd be 27, probably still paying the loan. If I haven't got somewhere safe by then, I'm in trouble. But I'd have a few years of pay to put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: keep the job, clear the smallest debt, and finish the bookkeeping certificate. Then look at public-sector finance or something that needs a person in the room, like helping people with benefit forms at the advice centre. I'd get some training paid for through the union. I'd still avoid chatbots unless I'm forced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier than the two-year one. Five years is enough to be hurt slowly instead of all at once, and a countdown is horrible, but it's one I can plan against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd avoid chatbots unless forced. What would force you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Petrov saying it's part of the job. Then I'd learn it, slowly, at lunch, with someone checking my work. I won't be the first one in the building to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting a business degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't borrow so much. Look at jobs that deal with real people's problems, like the advice centre, tax help or housing. If everything on screen is automated, the people who stand next to a human being in trouble will still be needed.

say: There's time to organise, so unions should push for **shorter weeks** and paid retraining.
I'd say it online, though I'm **no influencer**.
think: Five years means being hurt **slowly**, and I'd be 27 and still repaying the loan.
The **countdown** is horrible, but at least I can plan against it.
do: Finish the **bookkeeping certificate** and clear my smallest debt in year one.
Look at advice-centre and **public-sector** roles that need a person in the room.
feel: A bit **steadier** than the two-year case, with a countdown to plan against.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to be hurt slowly instead of all at once, and a countdown is horrible, but it's one I can plan against.
fieldNote: Adapts **only when forced**, and then slowly and with oversight.
Reaches for **people-facing** work as protection against automation.
Mood stays **anxious** because the debt and thin cushion remain.

steps.text: Finish the bookkeeping certificate Mr Petrov part-funds
Clear the smallest of my three loans first
Apply for advice-centre and housing-office finance roles
Ask the union to pay for a retraining course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd call a long runway, and I'd say governments have no excuse. I'd push for things like a shorter week, a basic income and a tax on the firms that profit. I'd argue it at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel nearly relaxed, which feels wrong. By 2036 I'd be 32, I might have cleared the loan, and I could have another trade. The fear is that I'd waste ten years doing the same invoice matching and then get the news at 32 with nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for a few years and finish the certificate, then train as a tax adviser or a debt adviser, work that talks to real people. I'd pay off the loan fast, rent somewhere without sharing, and start a pension. I'd try the AI tools once they're proven and everyone's using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, not calm. I'm good at worrying, so I'd find something. But the time helps a lot, and I'd feel I have a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you'd actually be glad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the gains were shared, yes. Four-day weeks, cheaper bills, no one sleeping rough because machines do the work. I think that's possible, but only if people push, not if we leave it to the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from using that decade well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear of change, I think. I'm the one who stays at the same desk for six years because it's familiar. My flatmate Joel says I should leave sooner. He's probably right.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so governments have no excuse.
I'd argue for a **shorter week** and a tax on firms that profit.
think: Part of me feels almost **relaxed**, which feels wrong.
I fear wasting ten years on **invoice matching** and meeting the news at 32 with nothing new.
do: Finish the certificate, then train as a **tax or debt adviser**.
Clear the loan fast and start a **pension**.
feel: **Calmer, not calm**, because the time gives me a say.
S4.quote: I'm the one who stays at the same desk for six years because it's familiar. My flatmate Joel says I should leave sooner.
fieldNote: Expects to adapt **only when forced**, which he names himself.
Sees a **shared-gains** future if workers push, in keeping with his politics.
Mood eases to **uneasy** because ten years allows him to plan and clear debt.

steps.text: Train as a tax adviser or debt adviser over five years
Pay the loan down fast and move into a one-person flat
Campaign for a shorter working week through the union branch
Try the accounting software once the whole office uses it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. I'd have no savings, a pass degree and a firm with no reason to keep me. What would help is a cap on student loan payments and a real income guarantee. I'd also want my union to have a seat when firms decide to automate. Even a promise of retraining on paid time would make it feel less like being thrown off a bus.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not lazy about technology. I'm cautious because I've watched cheap fixes cost people their jobs. Nobody asks young people like me what we think before they decide. I'm not against technology. I'm against being the person who pays when somebody else's shiny idea goes wrong.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against being the person who pays when somebody else's shiny idea goes wrong.
portrait: Adam is a **22-year-old** junior bookkeeper at a haulage firm, paying a heavy student loan from low entry pay.
He leans left and blames **lenders and employers**, not technology, for his pressures.
He avoids AI tools and new systems out of caution, and says so openly.
His first instinct in each scenario is **collective**: join the union and push for rules.
He moves from mild worry in the slow case to **alarm** when AGI arrives in two years, easing again with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he would have almost no savings and a plain pass degree.
whatWouldHelp: A **cap on loan repayments**, an income guarantee and paid retraining with a union seat when firms automate.
